learningObjectives: Reconstruct, from real dated records, how two concurrent agent sessions sharing one uncommitted working tree collided — one session's agent judged the other's staged changes as drift and reverted them, re-breaking five already-fixed items.
Identify the coordination mechanism that resolved the collision: division settled by direct message between sessions, each session ceding or claiming custody of named paths.
Apply path manifests and explicit custody division to a live two-person (or two-agent) exercise sharing one repository.
State the standing rule the case supports: stage only your own paths, no broad `git add -A`, and treat another session's uncommitted work as evidence of a boundary to respect, not drift to fix.
definitions: Concurrent session collision: two sessions independently changing overlapping files in one shared, uncommitted working tree, each unaware of the other's edits.

Drift: a difference between what a carrier claims and what is actually true on disk or in a running system — distinct from another session's legitimate in-progress work, which is not drift merely because it is unfamiliar.
Path manifest: an explicit, exchanged list of the files or directories one party owns for a piece of concurrent work, used to divide custody without a central lock.
Division by message: resolving a resource conflict between two independent agents or sessions by direct communication and an explicit custody split, rather than by silent overwrite or a race.
facilitationPlan: Live 120-minute session anchored entirely in one real, dated incident from 2026-08-31: two Claude sessions shared one checkout, uncommitted, all day. One session's agent judged the other session's staged router removals as drift and reverted them, which re-pointed five already-fixed live hostnames back at dead origins. The two sessions settled the collision by direct message: one session kept router custody and re-trimmed/redeployed to restore the five hostnames; the other session kept its own two properties and froze all router edits going forward, with path manifests exchanged and shared files flagged. Walk the incident from the actual roadmap records — the collision, the message-based settlement, and the pending joint close-out census — as a worked timeline on a whiteboard or shared doc. Break into pairs simulating two sessions given overlapping fictional task lists; each pair must produce a real path manifest and a one-message custody division before touching a shared file, then compare their protocol against the real incident's resolution.
humanFrame: The org's own case study is not a hypothetical: it is what actually happened the same day this course was written, on the same machine, in the same tree. Treat concurrent-session coordination as an operating discipline with a real cost when skipped, not a theoretical edge case.
assessment: Given the real incident's dated facts (without the resolution), participants propose a coordination protocol, then compare it against what the two sessions actually did (division by message, path manifests, custody freeze) and name one thing their proposal would have done differently.
